paras.speaker: THE CLERK
paras.text: [00:00] Case number 25-1274, Hikvision USA, Inc., Petitioner, versus Federal Communications Commission. [inaudible] Mr. Noveck for the Respondents, and Mr. Johnson for the Intervenor.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [00:24] Morning, counsel. Mr. Simeone, please proceed when you're ready. Argument of Timothy J. Simeone for Petitioner

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [00:30] May it please the Court, I'm Tim Simeone representing Hikvision. I'd like to start with just briefly addressing the language of the Secure Equipment Act and its rule of construction. I want to move quickly to talking not about what the statute says, but why it says it. Because I think one of the main objections to our very textual reading of the statute and of the rule is that it makes no sense in the real world. I want to have the opportunity, if I can, to show that it does make sense. So — I'm sorry, I grabbed my glasses. [pause] [unclear] mistake. Only needed them a very short amount of time. [01:31] So the rule of construction and the Act both, we think, actually mean what they say. So the Act doesn't grant — I'm sorry, the rule of construction doesn't grant authority over revocations, but it makes clear that by limiting the ban to future authorizations, Congress shouldn't be understood to have denied authority over revocations. [02:02] So the Act itself makes a textual distinction that we've emphasized. The Act distinguishes between authorization of a ban as to future equipment authorizations, but no authorization as to revocations. And again, that is just what the statute says. And I think it makes sense. And that's what I want to focus on: why does it make sense? [02:39] So the first reason is that at the time when Congress was considering the Secure Equipment Act, there was pending before the Commission the 2021 NPRM. That's in the joint appendix. And there, the Commission addressed both future authorizations and revocations. But the Commission's consideration of the two issues was at a very different stage. The NPRM affirmatively proposed to ban future authorizations, but it only sought comment as to whether and under what circumstances the Commission could revoke. And that included the Commission asking about whether it could use the regulation that's at issue here — 2.939, I'm going to call it subsection (a)(4); there are four subsections. So the Commission actually asked in the NPRM if it could use that subsection in the covered-equipment context. That's because the regulation was promulgated under Section 302. It had not been used outside of the interference context. And so the Commission was asking about that. [04:10] So at the time of the NPRM, the Commission was further along in its consideration of the future-authorizations problem than the revocations problem. And that's one of the reasons why Congress distinguished, in the text of the Act, between the two things. But we think it also helps to explain what the rule of construction is doing. The rule of construction is an indication that Congress wanted that process to Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 1 of 19 proceed. It wanted to get the benefit of the agency's thinking. So by including the rule of construction, Congress indicated that it had not decided the issue of authority —

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [05:00] I certainly understand the textual distinction, and I appreciate the contextual information that you're giving us. Where you just left off was that Congress hadn't made the decision about authority. I guess to me it's possible, at least, that the distinction that's definitely being drawn under the law doesn't have to do with authority, but it just has to do with something beyond authority. "We're going to take as a given that you, of course, have the authority" — I'm going to hypothesize — "to take measures as to existing products too. But you've got to think really carefully about this, because it's a big deal. There's a lot of stuff that's out there. Unwinding past transactions is going to be complicated. So don't think that right now you should go ahead and willy-nilly do that too, just as you would for future products. Take some time, figure this out with existing stuff, because it's complicated." But that's not about the authority, because it just seems like night follows the day that if you have authority as to new products, you should have authority as to existing products too, because they present the same kinds of harms that led to the ban on new products.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [06:10] They don't present the same kind of harms, and Congress was aware of that, right? The other point that I was going to mention goes directly to this. At the time of the Secure Equipment Act, Congress had just decided to narrow what equipment could be reimbursed under rip-and-replace — reimbursed through the federal fund. By doing that, Congress showed that some equipment is more concerning than others, and some of this equipment had been in use for a very long time. So — I think I've lost the other half of your question.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [06:58] But even that doesn't seem to me to go to authority. That goes to implementation of authority. And I've taken that — as far as implementation of authority goes, it's complicated. But in terms of whether there's the authority, as an antecedent matter, to take measures as to existing products —

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [07:19] So I think the problem there is, if it's an antecedent matter, you have to point to the antecedent. So if the Commission's theory here is that this just preserves some pre-existing authority, it needs to show where that authority is.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [07:35] So I guess on that issue — I think there's some force to your position. I take the point as to 302 and some — I have tried to work my way through those provisions, and I understand what you're saying about that. But it seems to me this case comes to us on the understanding that we take as a given that there's authority, wherever it comes from, as to future products.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [08:01] Right, that's established from the previous decision. And our position would be that comes from the affirmative grant of authority in the Secure Equipment Act.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [08:09] Exactly. Okay, so let's just take that as a given. So let's just say that's a given. Then why would it make sense to think that if it comes from the Secure Equipment Act, the SEA, that that wouldn't also carry with it authority as to existing products? It just wouldn't make sense to think that a Congress that wanted to give authority as to new products would have wanted to deny it as to existing products.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [08:37] There's a lot in there. I would start with the text of the SEA itself. Congress recognized that future authorizations and revocations were different things, right? It had a provision saying, "Do this now." And it had a provision saying, "We're not preventing you from doing this other thing." But I think implicit in that is: we're not preventing you from doing revocations if you have authority to do it. The text of the rule can't be read as an affirmative grant of authority, right? It says "nothing in this" chapter "shall" "prohibit." That's not an affirmative grant of authority. [09:24] So the text of the SEA actually distinguishes. You have future authorizations, you have revocations. One falls into the affirmative grant of authority: do this within a year. Congress could have said, "Do this within a year, and do that within a year." Or it could have said nothing, right, on your theory.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [09:53] What if Congress would have said, as to the second part — as to existing products — what if it explicitly said: "As to new products, [do this]. As to existing products, we just want you to think carefully about whether they're out. Think about that. And if you'd like to take those out, go ahead. If Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 2 of 19 you don't want to, then don't."

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [10:16] That's one of the theories that the Commission advances, right? That it was a congressional "the Commission may." Right? As to future authorizations, Congress said "the Commission shall." And the Commission here says, "We read the statute as saying, as to revocations, the Commission may." But you don't write a rule of construction to say "the Commission may." You write a rule of construction, in this case, to say: the fact that we only went so far here, the fact that we only gave authority over future authorizations — the parties here can't go to the Commission and argue the negative inference. Right? That's what a rule of construction does. It tells us how to understand the parts of the statute that come before. [11:17] So here, it's a rule of construction of the previous sections of the statute. And what it says — and I think it's talking to the Commission as much as the courts — it's saying: you still have this proceeding that I was talking about; that NPRM is still in front of you. And we don't want you to think we've taken authority away. We want to do exactly what you just suggested, Chief Judge. We want you to think carefully. [11:48] There's more to the story, I think, when you think carefully. And I hadn't gotten to my other point. But — so the other point contextually. So you have the NPRM. The NPRM actually, in a sense, doesn't take the position you described. The NPRM doesn't say subsection (a)(4) allows us to revoke because it allows us to not grant those authorizations. The NPRM says, "Can we use this?" It asks whether "we can use this." So the Commission's argument that Congress somehow adopted the regulation — the regulation can't itself expand the Commission's authority. The Commission can't expand its own authority, right? So the Commission very sensibly argues —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [12:41] Can I ask about — so the Commission amended its existing regulation to add the subsection (e) that's at issue here. Imagine they hadn't done that.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [12:57] Do you mean when they amended —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [13:00] Subsection (a), just to add the limitation language, in the 2025 order. 47 CFR 2.939 now has subsection (e), which I think comes out in —

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [13:15] Okay, okay. I'm sorry, I missed — go ahead.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [13:19] Let us — for purposes of this question, [assume] that you're right: (e) is no good, it's out. Couldn't they do the same thing under the pre-existing regulation — [that's] been in effect for quite some time — under subsection (a)(4)?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [13:38] That's what I'm talking about. I'm sorry, I may have been unclear. So subsection (a) (4) didn't have the language — the "revocation, withdrawal, or limitation." At the time of the Secure Equipment Act, there was nothing in the law anywhere contemplating limitations.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [14:05] I think I'm really confused here.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [14:07] So on my addendum, 26 —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [14:11] All right, I'm just looking at the actual thing itself. But sorry, is this the addendum to your brief?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [14:17] Yes, the addendum to the first brief.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [14:21] I don't have an addendum of — well, never mind. Got it. Which page are you on?

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [14:30] I'm just getting really confused about the addendum —

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [14:32] Not of the brief. So it's labeled at the top "47 CFR 2.939(a)." And so —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [14:44] That's not the current rule. [unclear] The rule has subsections (b), (c), (d), and (e). And (e) is the one that authorizes the bureaus to do what they did.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [15:03] Right, but the one — I mean, all of this is, of course — let me just maybe —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [15:09] So what you have on page 26 — right, that's what you're talking about, (a)(4) — Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 3 of 19 that long predated this legislation.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [15:20] Yes, but not as to limitation.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [15:23] So — I mean, the "limitations pursuant to paragraph (e) of this section." Okay. Right. So I think I understand your point. Right. So let's — I take your point. "[O]r place limitations pursuant to paragraph (e) of this section." So we can [set that aside]. But go ahead — why shouldn't they just use old 2.939, "the Commission may revoke any equipment authorization" for the reasons of (a)(4)? So this is right about limitation here and subsection (e).

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [15:55] This is exactly what they said in the NPRM that we were talking about.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [16:01] Sorry, I'm asking a much more direct question than that. I'm asking: why can't they? You haven't challenged the — you haven't said there's a lack of authority for old 2.939(a)(4). So you haven't argued that. But couldn't they have used that exact same power to do the revoking that they're doing here?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [16:23] That's what they asked if they could do in the NPRM.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [16:26] I think the answer is they already have the authority to revoke because of "conditions coming to the attention of the Commission which would warrant it in refusing to grant an original application."

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [16:36] That's promulgated pursuant to Section 302. There was no authority for that outside of Section 302. So what I'm saying is —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [16:47] So the old 2.939 was promulgated pursuant to a number of statutory authorities, including — but I'm just trying — I'm just asking kind of a factual question, to understand. Pretend we just have old 2.939(a). Could they not use that power to do the very revocations of past authorizations?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [17:11] And my answer is no. It depends on the statutory grant of authority, right? They can't expand whatever authority they have over equipment authorization — over revocations — by using the — they're essentially — let's go back to the Secure Equipment Act. We agree that the Secure Equipment Act distinguishes between future authorizations and revocations. And I just —

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [17:41] I just ask you — just to try to make sure I understand your answer to Judge Millett's question.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [17:49] So 2.939(a)(4) has been in place for a long time. And the question is: why couldn't that regulatory exercise of authority be used to do the exact same thing that's being done now? Your answer is it can't. And I thought the reason your answer is it can't is because you read 2.939(a)(4) as limited to a particular context — as limited to the context of radio interference or something like that. Is that not your answer?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [18:21] It's not exactly my answer. It's that wherever the Commission is trying to apply that regulation — whether it applies it to ten different places — in each context, there needs to be statutory authority. The regulation in this context doesn't exist because — going back to your original question — the Commission hasn't pointed to where. If we think of the Secure Equipment Act as preserving some previous authority that, for example, could be the authority for this regulation — right, if the idea is the Commission had this authority before, we want to know where. What statute? They for years have pointed to Section 302. They pointed to Section 302 here.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [19:13] What about 302 and 154(i) together?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [19:16] Well, I think —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [19:17] Or the Secure Equipment Act and 154(i) together.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [19:21] Well, this — right. 154(i) is, as all of the — this Court has held that 154(i) has to be used in conjunction with a specific delegation of authority to the agency, right? They have to point at what Congress told them to do, such that they can use that ancillary authority. Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 4 of 19

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [19:55] You take one, the Secure Equipment Act, that says we've got a really serious national security problem here, and so there shall be no more of these authorized out there. And then you also wrap in 302(a). You don't have to pick just one. We're going to wrap these together: 302(a). But doesn't that raise authority to prevent interference? And say — if the Commission says, very [well], in conjunction with protecting the national security, we also need to [stop the continued] marketing of existing authorizations —

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [20:36] I think our core objection to that is that it erases the distinction that Congress made in the text of the Secure Equipment Act. Congress granted a certain authority over future authorizations —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [20:52] It wasn't — to accept your reading, I think — I'm sorry, I just want to make sure I'm getting this clear in my head — we have to reject flat out the notion that, in having the authority prospectively to stop authorizations because of congressional determination — this is not our judgment, it's a congressional determination — that these products endanger the national security of the United States, there could not be an ancillary authority to that. That it could not be part of executing that function for the FCC to say: we also are not going to allow continued marketing and importation of previously authorized equipment, now that we know — whoops — we could never authorize that going forward, and that it's a national security problem. To say the two are completely divorced from each other —

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [21:48] So I want to get back to the question of the national security problem, because I don't think that's quite right. But I think —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [22:00] I'm sorry. I was just trying to say we can't — earlier on, Chief Judge Srinivasan had asked you about, sort of, as night follows day: if you can stop authorizing going forward for national security reasons, doesn't it follow that you could also say, whoa, wait, we already have this stuff in the system, let's not have any of it?

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [22:17] But what I wanted to say is, I think that erases the rest of the statute. That erases the rest of the Secure Equipment Act. Right? If Congress wanted to do that, all Congress would have had to do is say, "We want you to bar future authorizations," on that theory. That's all they had to say. But that's not what Congress said, and I think I know why Congress didn't say that. [22:47] Because at the time that they were considering the Secure Equipment Act, they had just decided that only Huawei and ZTE equipment would be eligible for reimbursement under the rip-and-replace program. That decision by Congress was a few months old at the time of the Secure Equipment Act. And so I think what they did in the Secure Equipment Act — how we make sense of the Act as a whole — is they said: we're giving you this authority prospectively. We're not saying that you can't ever do revocations. But what they were taking account of is, they knew that as to revocations — a revocation at the time, there was no limitation. A revocation was a full revocation. That meant you couldn't ever use the equipment. That meant it had to be removed and replaced. And that usually came with federal reimbursement. [23:58] So Congress had just solved this extremely large financial problem. It increased the rip-and-replace fund by a factor of five just for Huawei and ZTE. Then along comes this problem. And if they had given authority at that time to the FCC to just go ahead and revoke all the equipment authorizations, that was an enormous reimbursement problem that they didn't want to deal with. Our position is that Congress kicked this can down the road.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [24:33] Well, but I think you have to go further and say that Congress, in kicking the can down the road, said, "We're also kicking your existing 2.939(a)(4) authority." But where's the statute that authorizes that, in the context of the rule of construction? Little romanette (i) sounds exactly like 2.939(a)(4), pre-existing: "examining the necessity of review or revocation of any equipment authorization on the basis of the equipment being on the list described in paragraph (2)," which sounds like exactly — it has now come to the Commission's attention that we couldn't authorize this, so now we can revoke it. But I think we have to deal with it. I think you have to have a theory that says Congress not only said, "We're tabling that topic for now," but "we are also, through this language, expressing our view that your existing authority to revoke — your existing authority and your regulation — is now on hold too."

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [25:46] I think that's inconsistent with the first phrase of that section of the statute. It's not delegating authority. It's saying "nothing in this chapter" "shall" "prohibit" — Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 5 of 19

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [26:00] Right. So it said nothing [prevents you] from applying your existing regulation. But it doesn't say we're putting [it] over here, amending the regulations — but "we're not prohibiting you from" — which would — so a different procedure would allow them just to do exactly what they're doing here.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [26:26] Let me just make sure I understand. I think you're saying that the regulation has been previously authorized by some statute other than Section 302.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [26:36] I see nowhere in your [briefing] [you] raising [the] argument that old 2.939 — the 2.939 existing at the time of the Secure Equipment Act — was an unlawful regulation beyond the Commission's authority.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [26:55] I think it depends on the context where the Commission applies it, right? If it has the authority to revoke, it can certainly apply a regulation that revokes. But if Congress has —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [27:04] You think there's no underlying statutory authority to revoke in this context.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [27:07] That's exactly what I'm saying. I was trying to say earlier —

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [27:11] You think it has to be tethered to some specific statutory source of authority that allows you to revoke in this context, and that authority is non-existent.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [27:19] Right. And I don't think you can use 154 or whatever to fill that gap.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [27:24] If I — under your argument, what's the rule of construction? The rule of construction says nothing may be construed to prohibit the Commission from revoking. Is that a fair shorthand?

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [27:40] So then your view is: nothing may be construed to prohibit the Commission from revoking — but actually the Commission can't revoke.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [27:49] No, I don't think that's right. I think what this goes to is my point about the NPRM —

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [27:54] But grant the result — the result of your argument is that the Commission cannot revoke.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [27:58] No, the result of my argument is it goes back to the Commission in the pending NPRM, and the process continues, right?

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [28:07] But you think that there's not any statutory authority to revoke.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [28:13] Not here, no.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [28:16] Can I ask a version of this?

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [28:18] The question is: can they revoke for national security reasons? Right — I know that's shorthand for being on the covered list. Let's just say: can they revoke for national security reasons? And your position is they never could before this; they could not revoke for national security. So what they did in the Secure Equipment Act — your view is the one and only thing they did is confer, for the first time, authority to deny new approvals for national security reasons. And then you read the rest of the statute to say, "We are just not saying anything" [about] authority to revoke for national security reasons.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [28:53] Look to other pre-existing statutes. That's your argument.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [28:56] Yeah, but you think those other — I don't want to get you back [into it] — and you think that those statutes do not provide that authority.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [29:01] Well — and specifically, of course, for five years the Commission relied on Section 302. And they've now abandoned that. I mean, that's what was in the order. But I think the — [unclear] Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 6 of 19

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [29:14] Yes. Continue.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [29:16] Please, please.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [29:17] Sure. So I'm trying to synthesize this all for myself.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [29:24] And — [someone] cut me off. Okay, sorry. Sorry, my apologies. Okay, so you think it came in — you would agree — I think [that's what] some of these questions are [getting at] — you would agree that if all this statute said was [2(a)(2)] — "you now have authority to deny authorization based on national security reasons" — you would be in a worse position. Because that might allow us to say, implicitly, the authority to approve carries with it the authority to revoke. But you would say, no, they told you exactly what they want to tell you about revocation authority, and it's nothing but [a] distinguishing between the two things.

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [30:18] I actually think if 302 said what you postulated — I mean, isn't that essentially —

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [30:24] I don't think he said 302. I think he said 2. Just the SEA.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [30:31] I just think [you] would be in — if this just [said], "Now the FCC has authority to deny new authorizations for national security reasons," maybe you'd be in a more difficult position, because then it sure would be strange to think, well, Congress — they didn't address revocations; they must have thought you could revoke. But I think you would say they told you exactly what they [think]. There's nothing implicit about Congress's view on revocations. It's —

paras.speaker: MR. SIMEONE
paras.text: [31:08] Right. "We are not telling you a single thing about authority to revoke in this statute." That is our position. And my position is that they did that on purpose, right? They knew that immediate revocations would create an enormous problem. And maybe it was a compromise. Maybe Congress right now doesn't know what they think. And maybe those things, like what Judge Millett was asking — maybe the list here in this part of the statute was placed in there. You know, things end up in statutes for all kinds of reasons. But maybe it's placed in there by somebody —

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [31:38] I think what Judge Garcia helpfully added on — "for national security reasons," which I think was implicit, but it's really important to make it explicit. paras.text: [40:17] So would you agree, in the abstract, it would be a coherent thing for Congress to do, Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. paras.text: [46:50] Sorry — well, it's two, [not] (3)(B) —

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [48:00] That might help the night-follows-day [argument].

paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [48:03] Yes, I believe it's bolstering that. I think it bolsters that. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 11 of 19 [48:19] And my third point on this is that if you look at 2(a)(1) of the Secure Equipment Act, that's where Congress directed the FCC to act on the 2021 notice of proposed rulemaking. paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [48:53] At least — I'd like you to respond to this. You're right, the 2021 NPRM teed up both issues: authorizations, revocations. paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [49:13] So if you take a look at that NPRM at paragraphs 82 through 89, that's where the Commission addressed revocations. paras.text: [49:43] So do you think the affirmative conferral of authority to revoke — it's sort of implicit in 2(a)(2)? That's your argument?

paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [50:19] So I don't think that's the right construction of that paragraph (3), for the reasons that I've been trying to articulate, which is that if paragraph (3) was speaking about the FCC's substantive authority, first, I don't understand why it would be in a separate paragraph from (2). It says: if your boat is taking on water, the very first thing we want you to do, before trying to bail out any water, is plug that leak. And then after that, you're going to be free to deal with bailing out the water that's come on.

paras.speaker: JUDGE MILLETT
paras.text: [50:55] Sorry — but if it's just timing, you don't need (3)(B). (3)(A) covers timing.

paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [51:03] I think (3)(B) is sort of a belt and suspenders, to make sure nobody from (3)(A) draws an inference one way or the other. paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [51:59] I think that (3)(B) — it doesn't say "we're not saying one way or the other." It says it "shall not be construed to prohibit."

paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [52:07] Yes, I think that's right, Your Honor. Now, obviously, with the benefit of hindsight, could [this have been] written differently to be even more clear? And I just think it'd be very odd — given the national security context, given the backdrop of the existing regulations, given the NPRM that Congress was looking at — to have included this provision worded this way if Congress meant it to be read the way that Hikvision is trying to read or leverage it.

paras.speaker: JUDGE SRINIVASAN
paras.text: [52:42] Yeah, [on] this question. paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [53:01] I think that's right, Your Honor.

paras.speaker: MR. NOVECK
paras.text: [53:51] Sure. I think that's all correct. I mean, I hope it was clear from our brief, in that section where we said — this is, as you said, the fallback argument — that if you agree with us on the best reading of the Secure Equipment Act, you don't need to reach that. We certainly are. And I think, similarly, the Court's decision in Hikvision I didn't need to bite off some of these questions, because, from where we are now, I think Congress made very clear what it intended. [54:49] And then, Judge Garcia, I think we point to the cases at page 32 of our brief that establish the proposition that Congress, by directing an agency to take action, can amend existing law. So you asked the question: what if Congress acted on a belief [and the] belief was wrong? So in the Ninth Circuit case, the government had delisted, in part, gray wolves in some states but not others. And [the court said] the statute doesn't allow you to do a partial delisting; it's all or nothing. And it vacated that rule. And Congress came back, and Congress directed the agency to reissue that rule. And the challengers then said, "Well, that isn't good enough. The rule is still unlawful. You don't have the statutory authority." And what the Ninth Circuit said there, and this Court said in Friends of Animals, was: no, when Congress directs that sort of action, it amends the substantive law — or, this Court said, changes the reach of the underlying substantive law. So there's a whole host of different —

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [56:07] — although not actually written as a grant of authority either, it is a grant of authority, or can be construed as one, and Hikvision I is right.

paras.speaker: JUDGE GARCIA
paras.text: [56:18] If Congress really thought — it might be an odd state of the world — [that] the FCC can't revoke these existing authorizations, and Congress really had [something else] in its head — in the sequence of events you just described, that doesn't show the court was wrong. paras.text: [71:25] So that's true. But again, if we're talking in the abstract here: this regulation is just about whether you have equipment authorization. paras.text: [72:35] Mr. Johnson, for your three minutes.

paras.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
paras.text: [72:38] Thank you, Your Honor. May it please the Court, Tom Johnson appearing for the intervenor, Motorola Solutions. As this Court noted in Hikvision I, when it comes to the Secure Equipment Act, we do not need to rely on a presumption that Congress was aware of the pre-existing regulatory framework. To the contrary, the Act is the culmination of a years-long dialogue between Congress and the FCC about the appropriate way to address network equipment that poses a risk to national security. [73:06] In fact, this is the third time that challengers have brought to court an argument that Congress intended to limit or in some way repudiate the FCC's authority in this action — whether under the Secure Networks Act or now the Secure Equipment Act. And in both prior cases, a court has found that, in fact, Congress intended to ratify what the Commission was doing in the underlying proceeding. And there's unusually clear evidence of that here, Your Honors, and [that is] why this Court should reach the same decision now in Hikvision II. [73:40] So in the last appeal, this Court held that the Act's reference to the covered list indicated Congress's awareness of the underlying FCC docket and ratified the composition of that list as it appeared in that docket. So too here. I want to focus on a provision that hasn't gotten as much attention today: Section 2(a)(1). There, Congress directs the Commission to adopt rules in a proceeding called out by docket number and, to quote, "update the equipment authorization procedures of the Commission." That term, "equipment authorization procedures," is the title of Part 2, Subpart J of the Commission's rules, and it contains that revocation regulation that we've been talking about today, 47 CFR 2.939. [74:27] So just as the reference to the covered list in Hikvision I was viewed by this Court as a ratification of the content of the covered list as it appeared in that administrative record, this Court can look to Congress's awareness of — [and] explicit mention of — "equipment authorization procedures" in 2(a)(1) as ratifying those pre-existing procedures. And, Judge Millett, as you pointed out, one of those procedures, subsection (a)(4), pre-existed by many years the adoption of this Act. So that is the first textual indication. [74:58] I think the second textual indication is the one that this Court has discussed at some length, which is that the reference to authorizations contains within it an implied authorization to exercise the legal authority to repeal — or to revoke, rather. [That's] consistent with the opinion of the Ninth Circuit in China Unicom, [and] consistent with what they cited there, back to Myers v. United States and Chief Justice Taft's statement that the power to appoint includes the power to remove. I think those are two key textual indications that Congress was aware of and ratified that pre-existing regime before you get to subsection (3). Unofficial transcript — Hikvision USA, Inc. v. FCC, No. 25-1274 (D.C. Cir., argued Oct. 6, 2026) — Page 17 of 19 [75:38] So subsection (3) then removes any doubt that Congress was aware of the possibility of revocation authority. Congress is addressing it specifically. And what makes this, I think, a much easier case — Judge Garcia, [given] the kind of synthesis of the petitioner's case that you set out — I think we would have a much harder time of it if this were written as a sort of generic savings clause, the way you would typically see these written: "Nothing in here should be construed to have any impact on the Commission's prior Title III authority," something of that nature. But [look at] the fact that they are so specific, in two ways — so bespoke. [76:14] First, the timing mechanism we were talking about, where they're not simply saying "you're prohibited from doing it," but saying "you're not allowed to do it now, but you may do it in the future," including that language "nothing shall be construed to prohibit" at a later date — which I think, Chief Judge Srinivasan, you're right, kind of naturally implies authorization, more so than, as Judge Millett suggests in the question, potentially being agnostic as to the question. [76:43] And then I think the fact that, specifically, in both subsections of (3), [they are] calling out the basis on which they're contemplating revocation, right? "On the basis of the equipment being on the list." I think that removes doubt that what they might be potentially talking about is preserving prior interference-mitigation authority. If they wanted to say that, they might have been more general, as I said — talking about Title III authority generally. But they're specifically talking about a specific type of revocation authority. And if, in fact, that revocation authority did not exist — or, as counsel is now arguing here, if they simply wanted the FCC to explore it more — I think what would be effectively saved here, if you want to consider this a savings provision, would effectively be a null set. And there would be no reason for Congress to speak in this manner and say, "Not now; potentially later."
